title: ClinTutor-R1: Advancing Scalable and Robust One-to-Many Alignment in Clinical Socratic Education
one_liner: ClinTutor-R1 teaches a group by tracking each trainee separately and then planning the next question from the group's shared state.
lead: A clinical tutor for one trainee can focus on one confusion at a time. A tutor for six trainees cannot. Each trainee may misunderstand a different part of the case, and the group still needs to move forward together. ClinTutor-R1 tackles that group-teaching problem by keeping an internal record for each trainee and another record for the group's current agreement, so the next teaching move can help the whole room instead of only the loudest person.

problem.h2: Why one-on-one tutoring logic breaks in a group
paras: Clinical teaching on ward rounds is a group problem, not a private chat. A tutor hears several answers, sees different confidence levels, and must decide whether to probe one trainee, repair a shared mistake, or move the whole group ahead. A standard language-model tutor usually compresses that situation into one running conversation, which loses the differences between trainees because all answers are mixed together in one context.

That loss matters because a good Socratic teacher does more than answer questions. The teacher chooses the next question so that the weaker trainees catch up while the stronger trainees still have to reason. If the system cannot represent who knows what, it cannot choose the right next question, and the group drifts into either confusion or boredom.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Model each trainee's current understanding and the group's shared view separately, then choose the next question by balancing individual repair with group progress.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: separate trainee state from group state
paras: ClinTutor-R1 uses two levels of internal state. One level summarizes what each trainee currently seems to believe about the case. The second level summarizes what the group as a whole has accepted so far. That split helps because the tutor can detect when one trainee needs targeted follow-up and when the whole group is missing the same clinical step.

The paper also builds the surrounding training setup instead of only the final tutor. ClinEdu simulates group teaching sessions, and ClinTeach supplies large numbers of Socratic dialogues. That matters because the model needs repeated examples of group dynamics, turn taking, and teaching repair so that it learns when to challenge one trainee and when to redirect the full discussion.

stages.s: Clinical case plus several trainee replies
Update one state record for each trainee
Update one shared record for the group's current agreement
Pick the next Socratic question that best repairs the group state
Next teaching turn for the round

math.words: Score each candidate teaching move by combining how much it improves trainee understanding and how much it improves shared group agreement. Pick the move with the largest total improvement.
symbols: one candidate next question or teaching move
expected improvement in trainee i's understanding after asking q
expected improvement in the group's shared clinical understanding after asking q
weight that controls how strongly the tutor prioritizes shared progress versus individual repair

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Three trainees discuss chest pain. Trainee A misses the risk factors, trainee B misses the electrocardiogram step, and trainee C is mostly correct.
Candidate question 1: "What finding would make acute coronary syndrome more likely?" This gives gains [2, 0, 0] and group gain 1.
Candidate question 2: "What is the next bedside test we need before deciding disposition?" This gives gains [0, 2, 0] and group gain 2.
The tutor asks question 2 because it repairs one trainee's gap and moves the whole round forward at the same time.

math.note: The paper describes explicit internal reasoning about individual belief states and group consensus. This equation is a compact way to express the decision logic that the system is trying to learn.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small simulator with one clinical case, four trainee profiles, and a fixed scoring rule for teaching quality. Run two tutors on the same simulated round: a plain tutor that only reads the full dialogue text, and a group-aware tutor that keeps separate trainee records plus a group record. After each tutor turn, score whether the weaker trainees improved and whether the group reached the correct next clinical step.
The demo should show that the group-aware tutor asks better follow-up questions because it can target the missing concept without losing the group's overall path through the case.
demo.metric_eq: teaching_score = cohort_accuracy_after - cohort_accuracy_before ; group_progress = correct_shared_steps / required_shared_steps
demo.closing: The win is not only higher final accuracy. The win is that the tutor keeps the room aligned because it tracks each trainee and the shared discussion separately.

items.html: If the tutor misreads what one trainee knows, it may ask a follow-up that is too easy or too hard, because the next turn depends on the stored state for that trainee.

items.b: Putting too much weight on group agreement.
items.html: If lambda is too large, the system may push the group ahead before weaker trainees recover, because the scoring rule rewards shared progress more than individual repair.
ClinEdu can only teach the tutor patterns that exist in the simulator, so real trainees may behave differently if they ask less orderly questions or reveal confusion later than the simulator expects.

The evaluation includes static tests and interactive rounds so that the paper checks both knowledge quality and live teaching behavior, because group tutoring quality depends on turn-by-turn choices rather than on final answers alone.
